Recent progress in artificial neural networks has shown that when large models are trained on enough linguistic data, grammatical structure emerges in their representations. We extend this work to the domain of mathematical reasoning, where it is possible to formulate precise hypotheses about how meanings (e.g., the quantities corresponding to numerals) should be composed according to structured rules (e.g., order of operations). Our work shows that neural networks are not only able to infer something about the structured relationships implicit in their training data, but can also deploy this knowledge to guide the composition of individual meanings into composite wholes.

papers.title: Do Large Language Models Understand Logic or Just Mimick Context?
papers.research_question: Do LLMs understand logical rules to draw inferences, or do they 'guess' the answers by learning a type of probabilistic mapping through context?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs do not truly understand logical rules; in-context learning simply enhances the likelihood of correct answers. Altering context or logical terms significantly disrupts model outputs, indicating reliance on probabilistic associations.
papers.conclusion: While LLMs may improve their logical reasoning performance through in-context learning and methodologies such as COT, these enhancements do not equate to a genuine understanding of logical operations and definitions, nor do they necessarily confer the capability for logical reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Chain of Thought (COT) in-context examples markedly improve the performance of large-scale models on logical reasoning tasks.
Large models demonstrate resilience to distracting elements within in-context examples, while smaller models suffer notable declines in performance when standard in-context examples are not used.
Large models do not genuinely comprehend logical principles; they rely on probabilistic associations between input examples and outputs.
Modifying logical symbols and predicates leads to a low rate of successful adaptation across all model sizes, even with prompt-based or example-based guidance.
Example-based guidance (providing modified examples) improves the modification rate more than prompt-based guidance alone.
papers.limitation: The enhancement in logical reasoning from prompts and in-context examples remains marginal, and current pre-training based on next-token prediction may not be suited for logical tasks.
future_direction: Devising an alternative pre-training strategy tailored to the requirements of logical tasks.
Exploring methods to enhance the model's logical reasoning capabilities independent of context-based examples.
papers.abstract: Over the past few years, the abilities of large language models (LLMs) have received extensive attention, which have performed exceptionally well in complicated scenarios such as logical reasoning and symbolic inference. A significant factor contributing to this progress is the benefit of in-context learning and few-shot prompting. However, the reasons behind the success of such models using contextual reasoning have not been fully explored. Do LLMs have understand logical rules to draw inferences, or do they ``guess'' the answers by learning a type of probabilistic mapping through context? This paper investigates the reasoning capabilities of LLMs on two logical reasoning datasets by using counterfactual methods to replace context text and modify logical concepts. Based on our analysis, it is found that LLMs do not truly understand logical rules; rather, in-context learning has simply enhanced the likelihood of these models arriving at the correct answers. If one alters certain words in the context text or changes the concepts of logical terms, the outputs of LLMs can be significantly disrupted, leading to counter-intuitive responses. This work provides critical insights into the limitations of LLMs, underscoring the need for more robust mechanisms to ensure reliable logical reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: An Investigation of Neuron Activation as a Unified Lens to Explain Chain-of-Thought Eliciting Arithmetic Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: How can neuron activation in feed-forward layers of LLMs provide a unified explanation for the importance of various components in Chain-of-Thought prompts for arithmetic reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that analyzing the activation of reasoning neurons in feed-forward layers provides a unified explanation for why certain components (e.g., equations, textual explanation) in Chain-of-Thought prompts are important for eliciting arithmetic reasoning in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Neuron activation analysis provides valuable insights into the internal mechanism of LLMs for arithmetic reasoning and can explain prior empirical observations about Chain-of-Thought prompting.
papers.key_findings:
The paper discovered 113 neurons in Llama2-7B associated with arithmetic reasoning concepts such as logical connectors and arithmetic operations.
Corrupting the discovered reasoning neurons via random noise ablation leads to a significant performance drop, demonstrating their importance for eliciting reasoning.
The presence of equations and textual explanation in CoT prompts leads to higher activation of reasoning neurons, explaining their importance for performance.
Diversity of arithmetic operators in prompts leads to activation of a broader set of reasoning neurons, which improves model performance.
Incorrect in-distribution labels do not substantially affect reasoning neuron activation, while out-of-distribution labels cause different activation patterns and lower performance.
papers.limitation:
Neuron activation is necessary but not sufficient to completely explain LLM reasoning; interactions among components are also important.
The seven pre-defined concepts used may not cover the full scope of arithmetic reasoning, and activation can be faked by prompting.
Analysis was performed primarily on Llama2-7B; generalization to other LLMs may require different approaches.
future_direction: Future work should combine neuron activation analysis with other approaches like circuit analysis and top-down methods for a more complete understanding.
Extend the research to other LLMs and more comprehensive sets of reasoning concepts.
Systematically explore the potential of predicting LLM reasoning performance via neuron activation without human labels.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong arithmetic reasoning capabilities when prompted with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompts. However, we have only a limited understanding of how they are processed by LLMs. To demystify it, prior work has primarily focused on ablating different components in the CoT prompt and empirically observing their resulting LLM performance change. Yet, the reason why these components are important to LLM reasoning is not explored. To fill this gap, in this work, we investigate ``neuron activation'' as a lens to provide a unified explanation to observations made by prior work. Specifically, we look into neurons within the feed-forward layers of LLMs that may have activated their arithmetic reasoning capabilities, using Llama2 as an example. To facilitate this investigation, we also propose an approach based on GPT-4 to automatically identify neurons that imply arithmetic reasoning. Our analyses revealed that the activation of reasoning neurons in the feed-forward layers of an LLM can explain the importance of various components in a CoT prompt, and future research can extend it for a more complete understanding.

papers.title: Dissociation of Faithful and Unfaithful Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do LLMs recover from errors in Chain of Thought, and what factors affect faithful versus unfaithful recovery?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides evidence that LLMs have two distinct modes of reasoning (faithful and unfaithful) when recovering from errors in chain-of-thought, and these modes respond differently to factors like error magnitude and context.
papers.conclusion: LLMs have two distinct reasoning modes: one faithful and interpretable, and one unfaithful where the generated text does not accurately represent the internal reasoning. This challenges the reliability of chain-of-thought for model auditing.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs recover more frequently from larger errors than smaller ones.
Prior expectations of errors (via context noise or prompting) increase error recovery rates.
More evidence for the correct value in the context increases error recovery rates.
Faithful and unfaithful recoveries respond differently to interventions, indicating distinct mechanisms.
Different models (GPT-4, Claude-3 Opus, Llama-3) show varying patterns in faithful vs. unfaithful recovery.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to mathematical reasoning problems and does not investigate non-mathematical reasoning errors; additionally, the introduced errors may differ from naturally occurring errors.
future_direction: Understanding the mechanisms underlying faithful and unfaithful reasoning modes
Identifying factors that influence which reasoning mode is activated
Developing techniques to encourage faithful reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often improve their performance in downstream tasks when they generate Chain of Thought reasoning text before producing an answer. We investigate how LLMs recover from errors in Chain of Thought. Through analysis of error recovery behaviors, we find evidence for unfaithfulness in Chain of Thought, which occurs when models arrive at the correct answer despite invalid reasoning text. We identify factors that shift LLM recovery behavior: LLMs recover more frequently from obvious errors and in contexts that provide more evidence for the correct answer. Critically, these factors have divergent effects on faithful and unfaithful recoveries. Our results indicate that there are distinct mechanisms driving faithful and unfaithful error recoveries. Selective targeting of these mechanisms may be able to drive down the rate of unfaithful reasoning and improve model interpretability.

papers.title: ThoughtProbe: Classifier-Guided Thought Space Exploration Leveraging LLM Intrinsic Reasoning
papers.research_question: How are reasoning capabilities represented within LLMs’ internal activations, and how can these intrinsic abilities be effectively harnessed?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces ThoughtProbe, a classifier-guided search framework that leverages linear separability of thoughtfulness in LLM activations to improve reasoning performance without human intervention.
papers.conclusion: ThoughtProbe effectively leverages LLMs' intrinsic reasoning capabilities through classifier-guided exploration, advancing understanding and enabling practical application without human intervention.
papers.key_findings:
Thoughtfulness is linearly separable in LLMs' activation space, with a simple linear classifier achieving over 80% performance.
Different LLMs encode thoughtfulness differently across representation types and layers.
The classifier's logit consistently assigns higher scores to correct, thoughtful responses regardless of length.
The ThoughtProbe framework outperforms baselines on multiple math reasoning benchmarks.
Branch-aggregation selection outperforms single-branch selection and majority voting.
papers.limitation:
Fixed token lengths for segmenting intermediate thoughts may disrupt natural reasoning.
The gap between coverage and accuracy suggests room for improvement in answer selection.
Misalignment between training objectives (final outcomes) and guidance criteria (intermediate progress) may limit effectiveness.
future_direction: Explore more flexible, semantic-aware splitting criteria for tree node expansion.
Develop more sophisticated scoring metrics and aggregation methods for answer selection.
Explore step-wise feedback or hierarchical evaluation to better align classifier training.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained large language models (LLMs) have been demonstrated to possess intrinsic reasoning capabilities that can emerge naturally when expanding the response space. However, the neural representation mechanisms underlying these intrinsic capabilities and approaches for their optimal utilization remain inadequately understood. In this work, we make the key discovery that a simple linear classifier can effectively detect intrinsic reasoning capabilities in LLMs' activation space, particularly within specific representation types and network layers. Based on this finding, we propose a classifier-guided search framework that strategically explore a tree-structured response space. In each node expansion, the classifier serves as a scoring and ranking mechanism that efficiently allocates computational resources by identifying and prioritizing more thoughtful reasoning directions for continuation. After completing the tree expansion, we collect answers from all branches to form a candidate answer pool. We propose a branch-aggregation selection method that marginalizes over all supporting branches by aggregating their thoughtfulness scores, thereby identifying the optimal answer from the pool. Experimental results show that our framework's comprehensive exploration not only covers valid reasoning chains but also effectively identifies them, achieving significant improvements across multiple arithmetic reasoning benchmarks.

papers.title: Incremental Processing of Principle B: Mismatches Between Neural Models and Humans
papers.research_question: Do GPT-based autoregressive neural language models use Principle B to restrict their incremental coreference processing similarly to humans?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that GPT-based language models do not fully respect Principle B constraints in incremental coreference processing, unlike humans, and attributes this mismatch to statistical patterns in training data.
papers.conclusion: Autoregressive neural models do not uniformly process pronouns like humans; they learn only aspects of Principle B that have predictable reflexes in training data, suggesting certain aspects of human parsing behavior do not directly follow from linguistic data.
papers.key_findings:
For object pronouns, neural models show a negative Gender Mismatch Effect (GMME) when Principle B blocks co-indexation, meaning they expect pronouns to mismatch with grammatically unavailable antecedents, contrary to humans.
For possessive pronouns, models show positive GMMEs across the board, expecting gender agreement with all antecedents.
In cataphoric processing, larger models (GPT-J, GPT-3) show human-like behavior (no GMME when Principle B blocks), while smaller models (GPT-2 XL, GPT-Neo) do not.
Neural models underestimate the magnitude of processing costs compared to humans, even when qualitatively similar.
Analysis of training data (the Pile) shows skewed gender distributions that may explain the models' expectation of gender mismatches in certain positions.
papers.limitation:
Whether models truly 'interpret' the correct coreference relations is unclear, as techniques are limited.
Reliance on stereotypical associations between nouns and pronouns, which does not cleanly map to the real world.
Only English was investigated, limiting generalizability to other languages.
papers.abstract: Despite neural language models qualitatively capturing many human linguistic behaviors, recent work has demonstrated that they underestimate the true processing costs of ungrammatical structures. We extend these more fine-grained comparisons between humans and models by investigating the interaction between Principle B and coreference processing. While humans use Principle B to block certain structural positions from affecting their incremental processing, we find that GPT-based language models are influenced by ungrammatical positions. We conclude by relating the mismatch between neural models and humans to properties of training data and suggest that certain aspects of human processing behavior do not directly follow from linguistic data.

papers.title: From Black Boxes to Transparent Minds: Evaluating and Enhancing the Theory of Mind in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate and enhance Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from an interpretability perspective?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GridToM, a novel multimodal dataset for evaluating Theory of Mind (ToM), analyzes internal attention representations in MLLMs to show they distinguish perspective information, and proposes a training-free intervention method that enhances ToM performance by shifting activations along specific attention head directions.
papers.conclusion: The analysis of internal mechanisms shows that MLLMs develop attention heads capable of distinguishing perspective information and reasoning about beliefs, and targeted interventions based on these representations can significantly enhance their exhibited Theory of Mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in multimodal large language models can distinguish cognitive information across different perspectives, providing evidence of internal Theory of Mind representations.
A training-free intervention method, which adjusts activations in the direction of sensitive attention heads, significantly improves model performance on first-order and second-order belief tasks.
Multimodal large language models perform better on text-based ToM tasks compared to video-only tasks.
Linear probing reveals that belief states are linearly separable in the activation space of attention heads, indicating structured internal representations.
The constructed GridToM dataset enables comprehensive and interpretability-driven evaluation of ToM capabilities in MLLMs.
papers.limitation:
The tasks in the dataset are limited to first-order and second-order belief tasks within the ATOMs framework, while ToM theory encompasses a broader range of unexplored tasks.
Due to restrictions in accessing model code, the approach was only validated on a limited selection of MLLMs.
papers.abstract: As large language models evolve, there is growing anticipation that they will emulate human-like Theory of Mind (ToM) to assist with routine tasks. However, existing methods for evaluating machine ToM focus primarily on unimodal models and largely treat these models as black boxes, lacking an interpretative exploration of their internal mechanisms. In response, this study adopts an approach based on internal mechanisms to provide an interpretability-driven assessment of ToM in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Specifically, we first construct a multimodal ToM test dataset, GridToM, which incorporates diverse belief testing tasks and perceptual information from multiple perspectives. Next, our analysis shows that attention heads in multimodal large models can distinguish cognitive information across perspectives, providing evidence of ToM capabilities. Furthermore, we present a lightweight, training-free approach that significantly enhances the model's exhibited ToM by adjusting in the direction of the attention head.

papers.title: How Interpretable are Reasoning Explanations from Prompting Large Language Models?
papers.research_question: How interpretable are reasoning explanations from prompting large language models? The paper investigates this by evaluating the faithfulness, robustness, and utility of explanations generated by various prompting techniques.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces SEA-CoT, a prompting technique designed to improve the interpretability (faithfulness, robustness, utility) of reasoning explanations from LLMs, and provides a comprehensive evaluation framework for interpretability across multiple prompting methods and benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed SEA-CoT framework improves the interpretability of reasoning explanations across multiple dimensions, and the work provides a multifaceted evaluation methodology for assessing explanation quality in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SEA-CoT outperforms other prompting techniques (CoT, SC-CoT, QD, Self-Refine) in aggregate interpretability scores across faithfulness, robustness, and utility on commonsense reasoning benchmarks.
A single LLM setup for generating explanations and answers yields higher faithfulness and utility than a modular approach with separate explainer and predictor models.
Larger model sizes (e.g., Llama-2 70B) generally produce more interpretable explanations than smaller sizes, but SEA-CoT enables smaller models (7B) to outperform larger models using other prompts.
The selection of reasoning chains based on both entailment and keyword overlap (SEA-CoT) is more effective for interpretability than selection based on maximum probability or random choice.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a single LLM family (Llama-2) and does not explore other architectures or larger models like GPT-3.5/4.
The quality of automatic modifications (paraphrasing, mistake insertion, counterfactual generation) depends on the capability of the modifier models (GPT-3.5/GPT-4).
The work does not investigate techniques that ground LLM responses with external knowledge.
The work does not address the issue of self-hallucination in LLMs.
The work does not explore hybrid approaches like neuro-symbolic AI.
future_direction: Extend the investigation to transformers of different structures (encoder or encoder-decoder) and larger models like GPT-3.5/4.
Improve the quality of automatic modifications to explanations.
Incorporate external knowledge grounding into the interpretability framework.
Investigate hybrid approaches such as neuro-symbolic AI.
papers.abstract: Prompt Engineering has garnered significant attention for enhancing the performance of large language models across a multitude of tasks. Techniques such as the Chain-of-Thought not only bolster task performance but also delineate a clear trajectory of reasoning steps, offering a tangible form of explanation for the audience. Prior works on interpretability assess the reasoning chains yielded by Chain-of-Thought solely along a singular axis, namely faithfulness. We present a comprehensive and multifaceted evaluation of interpretability, examining not only faithfulness but also robustness and utility across multiple commonsense reasoning benchmarks. Likewise, our investigation is not confined to a single prompting technique; it expansively covers a multitude of prevalent prompting techniques employed in large language models, thereby ensuring a wide-ranging and exhaustive evaluation. In addition, we introduce a simple interpretability alignment technique, termed Self-Entailment-Alignment Chain-of-thought, that yields more than 70\% improvements across multiple dimensions of interpretability. Code is available at https://github.com/SenticNet/CoT_interpretability

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Interpretation of Multi-Step Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models perform multi-step reasoning tasks by using a reasoning mechanism or by memorizing answers from pretraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MechanisticProbe, a probing method that recovers reasoning trees from attention patterns, providing evidence that LMs perform multi-step reasoning mechanistically.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that reasoning trees can often be detected from LM attention patterns, supporting the claim that LMs may reason mechanistically.
papers.key_findings:
MechanisticProbe can recover reasoning trees from attention patterns of GPT-2 and LLaMA for most examples.
LMs identify useful statements in bottom layers and perform reasoning steps in higher layers.
Pruning attention heads that contribute to reasoning tree detection degrades performance, indicating a causal role.
Higher probing scores correlate with higher model accuracy and robustness to noise.
Finetuned models show clearer reasoning patterns in attention than few-shot models.
papers.limitation:
The study considered fairly simple reasoning tasks.
The analysis averages over attention heads, but heads may have different functions, especially in shallow models.
The analysis is limited to single-token prediction tasks and does not cover chain-of-thought reasoning.
future_direction: Explore more challenging reasoning tasks.
Analyze reasoning in chain-of-thought prompting settings.
papers.abstract: Yifan Hou, Jiaoda Li, Yu Fei, Alessandro Stolfo, Wangchunshu Zhou, Guangtao Zeng, Antoine Bosselut, Mrinmaya Sachan. Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2023.

papers.title: The LLM Language Network: A Neuroscientific Approach for Identifying Causally Task-Relevant Units
papers.research_question: Does specialization for language (and other cognitive domains) emerge in large language models, and what is the causal role of such specialized units?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired method to identify language-selective units in LLMs and demonstrates their causal role in language processing through ablation studies.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop specialized language units that are causally important for language processing, similar to the human brain, but specialization for other cognitive domains is less consistent.
papers.key_findings:
Language-selective units can be identified in LLMs using the same functional localization method as in neuroscience.
Ablating even a small percentage (e.g., 1%) of language-selective units causes significant performance drops in language tasks, while ablating random units does not.
The language-selective units in LLMs show similar response profiles to the human language network (e.g., stronger responses to sentences than to non-words, arithmetic, or code).
The language-selective units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language network than random units, especially when selecting a small subset of units.
Specialization for other cognitive domains (reasoning and theory of mind) is not consistently found across LLMs, with only a subset of models showing such specialization.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focused on models smaller than 13 billion parameters, which may not capture specialization in larger models.
They evaluated Theory of Mind and Multiple Demand units using only one benchmark each (TOMi for ToM and MATH for MD), which may not be comprehensive.
The localizers are adapted from neuroscience and may be constrained by the stimuli sets traditionally used in neuroscience.
future_direction: Expanding the study to include more models and a broader set of benchmarks.
Developing more targeted and robust localizers not restricted by neuroscience stimuli.
Analyzing varying numbers of selective units for MD and ToM networks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities on not just language tasks, but also various tasks that are not linguistic in nature, such as logical reasoning and social inference. In the human brain, neuroscience has identified a core language system that selectively and causally supports language processing. We here ask whether similar specialization for language emerges in LLMs. We identify language-selective units within 18 popular LLMs, using the same localization approach that is used in neuroscience. We then establish the causal role of these units by demonstrating that ablating LLM language-selective units -- but not random units -- leads to drastic deficits in language tasks. Correspondingly, language-selective LLM units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language system than random units. Finally, we investigate whether our localization method extends to other cognitive domains: while we find specialized networks in some LLMs for reasoning and social capabilities, there are substantial differences among models. These findings provide functional and causal evidence for specialization in large language models, and highlight parallels with the functional organization in the brain.

papers.title: Truth-value judgment in language models: 'truth directions' are context sensitive
papers.research_question: How does context affect the truth-value probes in large language models, and are these probes coherently incorporating contextual information?
papers.core_contribution: Truth-value probes are context sensitive but also sensitive to irrelevant information, and truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference.
papers.conclusion: Truth-value directions are context sensitive and causally mediate inference, but probes are not fully coherent.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-value probes are sensitive to context, but also to irrelevant information.
The type of errors (consistency errors) depend on the layer, model, and data.
Probes trained without premises (no-prem) still show context sensitivity, indicating that prior beliefs are not represented independently.
Instruction-tuned models show different error patterns (more E4 errors) compared to pretrained-only models.
Truth-value directions causally mediate natural language inference (intervention experiment).
papers.abstract: Recent work has demonstrated that the latent spaces of large language models (LLMs) contain directions predictive of the truth of sentences. Multiple methods recover such directions and build probes that are described as uncovering a model's "knowledge" or "beliefs". We investigate this phenomenon, looking closely at the impact of context on the probes. Our experiments establish where in the LLM the probe's predictions are (most) sensitive to the presence of related sentences, and how to best characterize this kind of sensitivity. We do so by measuring different types of consistency errors that occur after probing an LLM whose inputs consist of hypotheses preceded by (negated) supporting and contradicting sentences. We also perform a causal intervention experiment, investigating whether moving the representation of a premise along these truth-value directions influences the position of an entailed or contradicted sentence along that same direction. We find that the probes we test are generally context sensitive, but that contexts which should not affect the truth often still impact the probe outputs. Our experiments show that the type of errors depend on the layer, the model, and the kind of data. Finally, our results suggest that truth-value directions are causal mediators in the inference process that incorporates in-context information.

papers.title: REMA: A Unified Reasoning Manifold Framework for Interpreting Large Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we understand and localize reasoning failures in Large Language Models by analyzing the geometric structure of their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of the 'Reasoning Manifold' and the REMA framework, which diagnoses reasoning failures by quantifying and localizing the geometric deviation of erroneous internal representations from the manifold formed by correct ones.
papers.conclusion: REMA provides a novel geometric perspective for interpreting LLM reasoning, demonstrating that deviations from a 'Reasoning Manifold' are indicative of errors and allowing for the localization of failure points within the model's inference path.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states of both correct and incorrect reasoning exhibit low-dimensional structures (low Intrinsic Dimension).
Representations of erroneous reasoning consistently show statistically significant geometric deviation from the manifold of correct reasoning.
These deviations can be traced back to specific model layers (divergence points), revealing model- and task-dependent patterns of failure origins.
The relative deviation distance is negatively correlated with model accuracy, suggesting more difficult tasks lead to larger deviations.
Correct and error reasoning representations are highly separable in the latent space, as shown by UMAP/t-SNE visualizations and classifier accuracy.
papers.limitation:
The manifold approximation depends on the diversity and density of the correct samples.
Binary partitioning of samples into 'correct' and 'error' based on exact text match might misclassify 'nearly correct' reasoning.
future_direction: Building more precise manifold models using advanced manifold learning techniques.
Investigating the fundamental reasons for the formation of reasoning manifolds.
Exploring more fine-grained, confidence-based, or soft-scoring-based partitioning methods.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform complex reasoning and their failure mechanisms is a challenge in interpretability research. To provide a measurable geometric analysis perspective, we define the concept of the Reasoning Manifold, a latent low-dimensional geometric structure formed by the internal representations corresponding to all correctly reasoned generations. This structure can be conceptualized as the embodiment of the effective thinking paths that the model has learned to successfully solve a given task. Based on this concept, we build REMA, a framework that explains the origins of failures by quantitatively comparing the spatial relationships of internal model representations corresponding to both erroneous and correct reasoning samples. Specifically, REMA first quantifies the geometric deviation of each erroneous representation by calculating its k-nearest neighbors distance to the approximated manifold formed by correct representations, thereby providing a unified failure signal. It then localizes the divergence points where these deviations first become significant by tracking this deviation metric across the model's layers and comparing it against a baseline of internal fluctuations from correct representations, thus identifying where the reasoning chain begins to go off-track. Our extensive experiments on diverse language and multimodal models and tasks demonstrate the low-dimensional nature of the reasoning manifold and the high separability between erroneous and correct reasoning representations. The results also validate the effectiveness of the REMA framework in analyzing the origins of reasoning failures. This research connects abstract reasoning failures to measurable geometric deviations in representations, providing new avenues for in-depth understanding and diagnosis of the internal computational processes of black-box models.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: How does Chain of Thought Think? Mechanistic Interpretability of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Sparse Autoencoding
papers.research_question: Whether chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting faithfully reflects the true internal reasoning process of large language models.
papers.core_contribution: CoT prompting induces more interpretable, causally effective, and sparser internal features in high-capacity LLMs, enhancing reasoning faithfulness, but this effect is scale-dependent and minimal in smaller models.
papers.conclusion: CoT prompts induce more semantically coherent, causally effective, and sparser internal features in larger LLMs, but these effects are minimal in small models, highlighting the role of model capacity in reasoning faithfulness.
papers.key_findings:
CoT improves feature interpretability and semantic coherence in larger models (Pythia-2.8B) but not in smaller ones (Pythia-70M).
Activation patching shows that CoT features have significant causal efficacy in larger models, improving answer log-probabilities when patched into noCoT runs.
CoT leads to sparser residual activations and SAE feature activations, especially in larger models.
Random feature patching often outperforms top-K patching in large models, indicating that useful CoT information is distributed across many features.
The benefits of CoT are scale-sensitive, with clear effects only in models above a certain size threshold.
papers.limitation:
Activation patching targets only the residual activation of the final token and does not trace causal effects through the reasoning process.
Interpretation module relies on OpenAI's LLM-based scoring, which offers an indirect perspective and is not grounded in specific neurons or heads.
Experiments are restricted to Pythia-2.8B and smaller variants; findings may not generalize to larger models.
SAE-based feature analysis may introduce biases and miss distributed or entangled representations.
future_direction: Conduct token-level and path-based causal analysis, such as stepwise interventions and path patching.
Develop activation-grounded and causally-validated explanation methods, including probing, clustering, and patching.
Scale the framework to larger models and diverse architectures, and explore subspace patching and automated circuit discovery.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting boosts Large Language Models accuracy on multi-step tasks, yet whether the generated "thoughts" reflect the true internal reasoning process is unresolved. We present the first feature-level causal study of CoT faithfulness. Combining sparse autoencoders with activation patching, we extract monosemantic features from Pythia-70M and Pythia-2.8B while they tackle GSM8K math problems under CoT and plain (noCoT) prompting. Swapping a small set of CoT-reasoning features into a noCoT run raises answer log-probabilities significantly in the 2.8B model, but has no reliable effect in 70M, revealing a clear scale threshold. CoT also leads to significantly higher activation sparsity and feature interpretability scores in the larger model, signalling more modular internal computation. For example, the model's confidence in generating correct answers improves from 1.2 to 4.3. We introduce patch-curves and random-feature patching baselines, showing that useful CoT information is not only present in the top-K patches but widely distributed. Overall, our results indicate that CoT can induce more interpretable internal structures in high-capacity LLMs, validating its role as a structured prompting method.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
The inhibition-mover head subcircuit behaves invariantly across tasks, as predicted by the IOI circuit.
The negative mover head in GPT2-Medium exhibits more sophisticated behavior than in GPT2-Small, directly demoting the subject token.
papers.limitation:
Quantifying circuit overlap is complex and not fully addressed in this paper.
The generality of the circuit beyond the studied tasks is not confirmed.
future_direction: Understanding how commonly the mover circuit is used by GPT2 in other tasks.
Developing methods for quantifying circuit overlap.
Studying circuit reuse in larger models.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.

papers.title: On the Limits of Hierarchically Embedded Logic in Classical Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the limits of logical expressiveness in neural networks based on their depth? Specifically, can neural networks faithfully represent higher-order logical predicates?
papers.core_contribution: Proves that neural networks have a strict upper bound on logical expressiveness, where each additional layer can encode at most one additional level of logical reasoning, and depth n networks cannot represent predicates in Ln+1.
papers.conclusion: These results motivate architectural extensions and interpretability strategies in future development of language models.
papers.key_findings:
A neural network of depth n cannot faithfully represent predicates in Ln+1, such as simple counting over complex predicates.
This limitation arises from the null space induced during tokenization and embedding, excluding higher-order predicates from representability.
The framework offers a natural explanation for phenomena such as hallucination, repetition, and limited planning in language models.
Approximations to higher-order logic may emerge through interpolation of lower-order predicates, leading to incomplete or incorrect predicates.
There exist predicates that neural nets cannot distinguish, regardless of training, due to finite depth and width, highlighting inherent reasoning limitations.
future_direction: architectural extensions
interpretability strategies
papers.abstract: We propose a formal model of reasoning limitations in large neural net models for language, grounded in the depth of their neural architecture. By treating neural networks as linear operators over logic predicate space we show that each layer can encode at most one additional level of logical reasoning. We prove that a neural network of depth a particular depth cannot faithfully represent predicates in a one higher order logic, such as simple counting over complex predicates, implying a strict upper bound on logical expressiveness. This structure induces a nontrivial null space during tokenization and embedding, excluding higher-order predicates from representability. Our framework offers a natural explanation for phenomena such as hallucination, repetition, and limited planning, while also providing a foundation for understanding how approximations to higher-order logic may emerge. These results motivate architectural extensions and interpretability strategies in future development of language models.

papers.title: On the Generalizability of "Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals"
papers.research_question: Does the competition of mechanisms between factual recall and counterfactual repetition, as identified by Ortu et al. (2024), generalize to larger models, different prompt structures, and across domains?
papers.core_contribution: The attention head ablation method from Ortu et al. (2024) does not generalize well; its effectiveness varies significantly with model architecture, prompt structure, and domain.
papers.conclusion: The competition of mechanisms identified by Ortu et al. (2024) is not fully generalizable; experimental findings in mechanistic interpretability are highly dependent on the specific model, prompt structure, and domain.
papers.key_findings:
Successfully reproduced the original findings on GPT-2 small and Pythia 6.9B regarding positional information encoding, attention block dominance, and attention head specialization.
In Llama 3.1 8B, attention head specialization is greatly reduced, and the logit lens method shows limited early-layer activity and a sharp final-layer activation.
Changing the prompt structure to a question-answering format reduces the model's propensity to repeat the counterfactual, indicating sensitivity to repetition.
The choice of premise word (e.g., 'Redefine', 'Validate') affects the rate of factual vs. counterfactual predictions and the effectiveness of attention head ablation.
The effectiveness of the proposed attention head ablation varies across domains; it works best for domains where the factual token is leaked in the subject (e.g., 'Autos and Vehicles') and fails for others.
papers.limitation:
The logit lens method may be unreliable for larger models like Llama 3.1 8B, potentially failing to capture early-layer mechanisms.
The filtered MQuAKE dataset used for domain analysis is very small (228 prompts), limiting definitive conclusions.
Most extended findings rely on GPT-2 small and a dataset derived from Ortu et al. (2024), limiting generalizability to other models and datasets.
future_direction: Investigate whether larger models distribute work more evenly across heads or if newer interpretability techniques (e.g., circuit analysis, tuned lens) are needed to capture their mechanisms.
Conduct a deeper analysis of why certain dataset domains impact attention head activation, distinguishing between token leakage, topic words, and task difficulty.
Extend the findings to different, larger datasets and models, as well as new prompt structures and premise words.
papers.abstract: We present a reproduction study of "Competition of Mechanisms: Tracing How Language Models Handle Facts and Counterfactuals" (Ortu et al., 2024), which investigates competition of mechanisms in language models between factual recall and counterfactual in-context repetition. Our study successfully reproduces their primary findings regarding the localization of factual and counterfactual information, the dominance of attention blocks in mechanism competition, and the specialization of attention heads in handling competing information. We reproduce their results on both GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) and Pythia 6.9B (Biderman et al., 2023). We extend their work in three significant directions. First, we explore the generalizability of these findings to even larger models by replicating the experiments on Llama 3.1 8B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), discovering greatly reduced attention head specialization. Second, we investigate the impact of prompt structure by introducing variations where we avoid repeating the counterfactual statement verbatim or we change the premise word, observing a marked decrease in the logit for the counterfactual token. Finally, we test the validity of the authors' claims for prompts of specific domains, discovering that certain categories of prompts skew the results by providing the factual prediction token as part of the subject of the sentence. Overall, we find that the attention head ablation proposed in Ortu et al. (2024) is ineffective for domains that are underrepresented in their dataset, and that the effectiveness varies based on model architecture, prompt structure, domain and task.

papers.title: Revisiting In-context Learning Inference Circuit in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the inference circuit that explains the observed phenomena of in-context learning in large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a comprehensive 3-step inference circuit (input text encode, semantics merge, feature retrieval and copy) to characterize the inference dynamics of in-context learning in large language models, and provides empirical evidence that it captures many observed ICL phenomena and is a dominant mechanism.
papers.conclusion: The proposed 3-step inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during in-context learning, providing a comprehensive and practical explanation of ICL inference in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Large language models encode input text into linear, task-relevant representations in the hidden states of forerunner tokens, and this encoding is enhanced by demonstrations.
Forerunner token heads copy text representations into label tokens without selectivity, forming joint representations of label semantics and text features.
Induction heads retrieve label representations similar to the query in task-specific subspaces and copy them to the query, enabling ICL prediction.
The proposed circuit explains phenomena such as positional bias, noise robustness, and demonstration saturation in ICL.
Ablation analysis shows the circuit is a dominant mechanism for ICL, but bypass mechanisms exist in parallel.
papers.limitation: The proposed circuit may not generalize to in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios, where the query's ground-truth label is not present in the demonstrations.
future_direction: Exploring different inference dynamics in in-weight learning (IWL) scenarios.
papers.abstract: In-context Learning (ICL) is an emerging few-shot learning paradigm on Language Models (LMs) with inner mechanisms un-explored. There are already existing works describing the inner processing of ICL, while they struggle to capture all the inference phenomena in large language models. Therefore, this paper proposes a comprehensive circuit to model the inference dynamics and try to explain the observed phenomena of ICL. In detail, we divide ICL inference into 3 major operations: (1) Input Text Encode: LMs encode every input text (in the demonstrations and queries) into linear representation in the hidden states with sufficient information to solve ICL tasks. (2) Semantics Merge: LMs merge the encoded representations of demonstrations with their corresponding label tokens to produce joint representations of labels and demonstrations. (3) Feature Retrieval and Copy: LMs search the joint representations of demonstrations similar to the query representation on a task subspace, and copy the searched representations into the query. Then, language model heads capture these copied label representations to a certain extent and decode them into predicted labels. Through careful measurements, the proposed inference circuit successfully captures and unifies many fragmented phenomena observed during the ICL process, making it a comprehensive and practical explanation of the ICL inference process. Moreover, ablation analysis by disabling the proposed steps seriously damages the ICL performance, suggesting the proposed inference circuit is a dominating mechanism. Additionally, we confirm and list some bypass mechanisms that solve ICL tasks in parallel with the proposed circuit.

papers.title: Probing the Geometry of Truth: Consistency and Generalization of Truth Directions in LLMs Across Logical Transformations and Question Answering Tasks
papers.research_question: Do LLMs universally represent truthfulness as a linear feature (truth direction)? Are simple probing techniques sufficiently expressive to identify truth directions? How does the truth direction generalize across logical transformations and question answering tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Consistent truth directions only emerge in capable LLMs and can be identified with simple linear probes; these probes generalize effectively to logical transformations, question answering, in-context learning, and external knowledge sources.
papers.conclusion: Truth directions are present in capable LLMs, can be identified with simple probes, and generalize well, highlighting their potential for eliciting latent knowledge and improving trust in LLM outputs.
papers.key_findings:
Not all LLMs exhibit consistent truth directions; this property is correlated with model capability, with stronger representations in more capable models.
Simple probes (linear SVM, logistic regression, MLP, mass-mean) are sufficient to identify truth directions when they exist.
Truthfulness probes generalize across logical negation, conjunction, and disjunction.
Truthfulness probes trained on atomic statements generalize to question answering tasks (MMLU, TriviaQA) and contextual knowledge tasks (SciQ, BoolQ, XSum).
Truthfulness probes can be used for selective question answering to filter out false answers, improving answer quality.
papers.limitation:
The term 'truth' may not be exactly what the probes measure; they likely capture an overlap between widely accepted human beliefs and objective truths.
Generalization is only tested on short-form QA; long-form QA and instruction-following tasks are not studied.
The causality of truthfulness probes is unclear; they may capture spuriously-correlated features rather than the target feature.
Computational resources limited evaluation to models up to Llama-3.1-70B, leaving more advanced models like GPT-4 untested.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more complex scenarios such as long-form QA and instruction-following tasks.
Study the causal implications of truth directions to guide LLMs toward more truthful responses.
Test the hypothesis on more advanced models like GPT-4.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on extensive datasets that encapsulate substantial world knowledge. However, their outputs often include confidently stated inaccuracies. Earlier works suggest that LLMs encode truthfulness as a distinct linear feature, termed the "truth direction", which can classify truthfulness reliably. We address several open questions about the truth direction: (i) whether LLMs universally exhibit consistent truth directions; (ii) whether sophisticated probing techniques are necessary to identify truth directions; and (iii) how the truth direction generalizes across diverse contexts. Our findings reveal that not all LLMs exhibit consistent truth directions, with stronger representations observed in more capable models, particularly in the context of logical negation. Additionally, we demonstrate that truthfulness probes trained on declarative atomic statements can generalize effectively to logical transformations, question-answering tasks, in-context learning, and external knowledge sources. Finally, we explore the practical application of truthfulness probes in selective question-answering, illustrating their potential to improve user trust in LLM outputs. These results advance our understanding of truth directions and provide new insights into the internal representations of LLM beliefs. Our code is public at https://github.com/colored-dye/truthfulness_probe_generalization

papers.title: Reason to Rote: Rethinking Memorization in Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize label noise, and why does such memorization not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization of noisy labels in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, with memories stored via distributed encoding and outlier heuristics in neurons.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that memorization of label noise builds on existing reasoning mechanisms, using distributed encoding and outlier heuristics, explaining the phenomenon of benign memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Models first learn to generalize on noisy training instances (predicting correct labels) before memorizing the noisy labels.
Even when producing memorized noisy labels, models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs corresponding to the correct labels.
Memorization and generalization circuits substantially overlap, indicating memorization builds on existing generalization mechanisms.
Memorization uses distributed encoding across multiple input tokens and intermediate results rather than a simple lookup.
In the FDA task, memorization occurs via 'outlier heuristics' where higher-layer MLP neurons slightly shift their activation patterns to fit noisy labels.
papers.limitation:
Focus on relatively small language models; larger models might exhibit different behaviors.
Models trained from scratch, so influence of pretraining data is not considered.
Examination of implicit reasoning without explicit solution steps; not studying models with explicit chain-of-thought.
future_direction: Study memorization in larger models
Investigate effect of pretraining on memorization and reasoning
Study memorization in models with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models readily memorize arbitrary training instances, such as label noise, yet they perform strikingly well on reasoning tasks. In this work, we investigate how language models memorize label noise, and why such memorization in many cases does not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities. Using two controllable synthetic reasoning datasets with noisy labels, four-digit addition (FDA) and two-hop relational reasoning (THR), we discover a reliance of memorization on generalizable reasoning mechanisms: models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs even when retrieving memorized noisy labels, and intervening reasoning adversely affects memorization. We further show that memorization operates through distributed encoding, i.e., aggregating various inputs and intermediate results, rather than building a look-up mechanism from inputs to noisy labels. Moreover, our FDA case study reveals memorization occurs via outlier heuristics, where existing neuron activation patterns are slightly shifted to fit noisy labels. Together, our findings suggest that memorization of label noise in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, shedding lights on the intriguing phenomenon of benign memorization.

papers.title: When Less Language is More: Language-Reasoning Disentanglement Makes LLMs Better Multilingual Reasoners
papers.research_question: Can reasoning and language processing in LLMs be disentangled to improve multilingual reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reasoning and language can be disentangled in LLMs by ablating language-specific components in hidden states, leading to improved multilingual reasoning performance across diverse models and languages.
papers.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that language and reasoning are separable in LLMs, and the proposed training-free intervention provides a lightweight and interpretable strategy for improving cross-lingual generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Language-reasoning disentanglement via activation ablation consistently improves multilingual reasoning performance across 10 open-weight LLMs and 11 typologically diverse languages.
There is a negative correlation between language-specific activation and reasoning accuracy; removing language-specific signals improves reasoning.
Middle layers are most effective for disentanglement, improving reasoning while preserving language fidelity, whereas upper-layer ablation degrades output fluency.
The training-free intervention achieves comparable or superior results to post-training methods like supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.
Low-resource languages show a trade-off: reasoning improves with ablation, but language fidelity drops more sharply than in high-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
After ablation, models tend to default to English, which may reduce language fidelity, especially for low-resource languages.
The exact ratios of pretraining data for different languages are unknown, which limits a definitive explanation of the convergence phenomenon.
future_direction: Further investigation into the convergence of non-English representations to English after ablation.
Exploring adaptive ablation strategies to balance reasoning improvement and language fluency for low-resource languages.
Combining the training-free intervention with post-training methods for enhanced multilingual reasoning.
papers.abstract: Multilingual reasoning remains a significant challenge for large language models (LLMs), with performance disproportionately favoring high-resource languages. Drawing inspiration from cognitive neuroscience, which suggests that human reasoning functions largely independently of language processing, we hypothesize that LLMs similarly encode reasoning and language as separable components that can be disentangled to enhance multilingual reasoning. To evaluate this, we perform a causal intervention by ablating language-specific representations at inference time. Experiments on 10 open-weight LLMs spanning 11 typologically diverse languages show that this language-specific ablation consistently boosts multilingual reasoning performance. Layer-wise analyses further confirm that language and reasoning representations can be effectively disentangled throughout the model, yielding improved multilingual reasoning capabilities, while preserving top-layer language features remains essential for maintaining linguistic fidelity. Compared to post-training methods such as supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning, our training-free language-reasoning disentanglement achieves comparable or superior results with minimal computational overhead. These findings shed light on the internal mechanisms underlying multilingual reasoning in LLMs and suggest a lightweight and interpretable strategy for improving cross-lingual generalization.

papers.title: What Does Loss Optimization Actually Teach, If Anything? Knowledge Dynamics in Continual Pre-training of LLMs
papers.research_question: How does loss optimization during continual pre-training (CPT) relate to the acquisition and retention of factual knowledge in LLMs, and does it provide a reliable signal for learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that loss optimization is misaligned with knowledge acquisition in continual pre-training (CPT); factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic despite monotonic loss decrease, and circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of internal knowledge pathways.
papers.conclusion: Loss optimization is not a reliable indicator of learning in CPT; probe-based trajectories reveal narrow learning windows invisible to loss curves, motivating task-based stopping criteria.
papers.key_findings:
Optimization and learning systematically diverge: loss decreases monotonically while factual knowledge acquisition is unstable and non-monotonic.
Acquired facts are rarely consolidated; learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure (entity frequency).
Out-of-domain (OOD) task performance degrades from early epochs during CPT.
Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, explaining narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) provides a much higher upper bound for factual recall, indicating the limitation is in the optimization process, not the data.
future_direction: Novel training objectives, evaluation protocols, and diagnostic tools that make learning dynamics observable during model adaptation.
Task-based stopping criteria that rely on task-level performance rather than next-token prediction.
papers.abstract: Continual Pre-Training (CPT) is widely used for acquiring and updating factual knowledge in LLMs. This practice treats loss as a proxy for knowledge learning, while offering no grounding into how it changes during training. We study CPT as a knowledge learning process rather than a solely optimization problem. We construct a controlled, distribution-matched benchmark of factual documents and interleave diagnostic probes directly into the CPT loop, enabling epoch-level measurement of knowledge acquisition dynamics and changes in Out-Of-Domain (OOD) general skills (e.g., math). We further analyze how CPT reshapes knowledge circuits during training. Across three instruction-tuned LLMs and multiple CPT strategies, optimization and learning systematically diverge as loss decreases monotonically while factual learning is unstable and non-monotonic. Acquired facts are rarely consolidated, learning is strongly conditioned on prior exposure, and OOD performance degrades from early epochs. Circuit analysis reveals rapid reconfiguration of knowledge pathways across epochs, providing an explanation for narrow acquisition windows and systematic forgetting. These results show that loss optimization is misaligned with learning progress in CPT and motivate evaluation of stopping criteria based on task-level learning dynamics.

papers.title: Who Reasons in the Large Language Models?
papers.research_question: A critical open question is whether reasoning abilities stem from the entire model, specific modules, or are merely artifacts of overfitting.
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes that the output projection (o_proj) in the Transformer's multi-head self-attention is primarily responsible for reasoning capabilities in LLMs, and introduces Stethoscope for Networks (SfN), a suite of diagnostic tools to probe and analyze internal behaviors, providing evidence for this hypothesis.
papers.conclusion: The work hypothesizes that the output projection (o_proj) module plays a central role in enabling reasoning capabilities in LLMs. The proposed Stethoscope for Networks (SfN) provides diagnostic tools that offer evidence for this hypothesis and open new directions for efficient and modular LLM training.
papers.key_findings:
The o_proj module exhibits the largest or second-largest weight changes during reasoning fine-tuning across model sizes (Delta Stethoscope).
Merging only the o_proj modules from a reasoning model into a base model can improve reasoning ability without further tuning (Merge Stethoscope).
Fine-tuning only o_proj (and layernorm, embed_tokens, lm_head) can achieve strong reasoning performance, with faster training and lower memory usage compared to full fine-tuning (Freeze Stethoscope).
Destroying o_proj does not harm conversational ability, while destroying MLP components or q/k_proj severely degrades it, suggesting a division of labor (Destruction Stethoscope).
The findings suggest o_proj is crucial for reasoning, while other modules primarily support conversational fluency.
papers.limitation:
Findings are primarily based on a limited set of model families and reasoning benchmarks, and may not generalize to all architectures or tasks.
Some diagnostic results rely on qualitative assessments rather than statistical validation.
A theoretical understanding of o_proj's function in reasoning remains to be established.
papers.abstract: Despite the impressive performance of large language models (LLMs), the process of endowing them with new capabilities--such as mathematical reasoning--remains largely empirical and opaque. A critical open question is whether reasoning abilities stem from the entire model, specific modules, or are merely artifacts of overfitting. In this work, we hypothesize that the reasoning capabilities in well-trained LLMs are primarily attributed to the output projection module (oproj) in the Transformer's multi-head self-attention (MHSA) mechanism. To support this hypothesis, we introduce Stethoscope for Networks (SfN), a suite of diagnostic tools designed to probe and analyze the internal behaviors of LLMs. Using SfN, we provide both circumstantial and empirical evidence suggesting that oproj plays a central role in enabling reasoning, whereas other modules contribute more to fluent dialogue. These findings offer a new perspective on LLM interpretability and open avenues for more targeted training strategies, potentially enabling more efficient and specialized LLMs.

papers.title: Neural Natural Language Inference Models Partially Embed Theories of\n Lexical Entailment and Negation
papers.research_question: Whether neural models for Natural Language Inference (NLI) can learn the compositional interactions between lexical entailment and negation.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT models, after fine-tuning on MoNLI, can learn to reason about lexical entailment and negation, and structural evaluations indicate they implement an algorithm for monotonicity reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT models can learn the compositional interactions between lexical entailment and negation, both behaviorally and structurally.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on general NLI datasets fail on MoNLI examples with negation.
Fine-tuning on MoNLI enables models to generalize to new lexical items in negated contexts.
Probes show that BERT representations correlate with lexical entailment relations.
Intervention experiments show that BERT's causal dynamics mirror the monotonicity algorithm on subsets of MoNLI.
BERT at least partially embeds a theory of lexical entailment and negation at an algorithmic level.
papers.limitation:
The interchange intervention methodology is not yet formally grounded.
The analysis only considered one location for interventions and may not capture all causal dynamics.
papers.abstract:
We address whether neural models for Natural Language Inference (NLI) can
learn the compositional interactions between lexical entailment and negation,
using four methods: the behavioral evaluation methods of (1) challenge test
sets and (2) systematic generalization tasks, and the structural evaluation
methods of (3) probes and (4) interventions. To facilitate this holistic
evaluation, we present Monotonicity NLI (MoNLI), a new naturalistic dataset
focused on lexical entailment and negation. In our behavioral evaluations, we
find that models trained on general-purpose NLI datasets fail systematically on
